newsitem.title: USA: Senate approves release of family planning aid.
newsitem.headline: Senate approves release of family planning aid.

text.p: The Senate voted on Tuesday to speed up release of international family planning funds, handing President Bill Clinton a victory in the first abortion-related debate of the new Congress.

By a 53-46 vote, the Senate joined the House of Representatives in approving a joint resolution allowing spending of $385 million in previously appropriated funds to start on March 1 instead of July 1.
Family planning and pro-choice groups hailed the vote, in which 11 Republicans joined 42 Democrats to support release of the funds and 44 Republicans and two Democrats voted against.

Under a compromise accord reached last year, Congress was required to vote on the resolution following a certification by Clinton that the delay in funding was having a negative impact on population programs.
Its passage allows the aid to be disbursed at the rate of 8 percent a month starting in March, five months after the opening of the 1997 fiscal year.
Opponents of the resolution said it would result in making extra funding of $123 million available to organizations that supported abortions.
Its supporters argued that continuing to hold up the money would result in more abortions.

The Senate did not act on a House-approved measure that would reimpose the policy of the Ronald Reagan and George Bush administrations denying funds for family planning groups that perform or advocate abortion, even if they use their own funds for that purpose.
Clinton scrapped that policy shortly after he became president. U.S. law bars American aid funds from being used directly for abortions.
White House spokesman Mike McCurry said Clinton was pleased by the bipartisan Senate vote and called it "a victory for women, children and families all over the world."

Gloria Feldt, president of the Planned Parenthood Federation of America, called the Senate action "an enormous victory for women" and said it marked the Senate's first stand-alone vote on family planning in a decade.
Maureen Malloy Ferguson of the National Right to Life Committee said the closeness of the vote showed the growing controversy of a program that she said helped promote abortion.

The House, which in the past has taken a more conservative stance on abortion issues, approved the resolution on Feb 13 by a 220-209 vote. Senate approval had been seen as likely, although last November's elections made the Senate more conservative.

The abortion issue is expected to be hotly contested again this year as Congress considers the 1998 foreign aid bill and when Republicans launch a new effort to try to outlaw certain late-term abortion procedures for U.S. women.
